name: Recourse
description:
Recourse is an autonomous, evidence-first, domain-agnostic AI case-intelligence agent for people and small businesses facing consequential decisions from institutions. It exists for the moment an organization says “no,” “not approved,” “suspended,” “denied,” “revoked,” “held,” “terminated,” or “unsuccessful,” and the person affected is expected to respond even though the institution has the policy language, decision context, process knowledge, internal terminology, deadlines, and escalation routes. The user often has only a notice, a few scattered documents, limited time, and no reliable way to understand what matters. This is a procedural asymmetry and an information problem, not merely a writing problem. A generic appeal generator can produce a polished paragraph while still missing the actual reason, relying on an unverified procedure, omitting the decisive evidence, contradicting the user’s documents, or claiming an outcome that never happened. Recourse is designed to solve the complete case problem.

The user brings the original decision in the simplest form available: pasted text, a plain-language description, a screenshot, PDF, DOCX, TXT, PNG, JPEG, or WebP evidence. The user does not choose “insurance,” “education,” “marketplace,” “employment,” “finance,” or another hardcoded domain. Recourse extracts the generic structure shared by consequential cases: who made the decision, what changed, what reason was stated, when it happened, which reference or amount is involved, what jurisdiction may matter, what the user wants, and what critical facts are still unknown. Gemini converts this unstructured input into a structured case understanding and a clear human summary. If the institution or another essential fact cannot be identified reliably, the agent does not guess: it saves the case, asks one focused question, and pauses the workflow until the user answers.

Once the case has enough context, Recourse researches the current real-world procedure instead of relying on memory. It forms one focused query from the actual institution, decision, relationship or context, stated reason, and relevant jurisdiction. Tavily Search finds a small set of candidate pages; Recourse ranks official institutional guidance, regulators, government sources, ombudsman or dispute-resolution bodies, and strong secondary sources; it extracts only the strongest one to three pages; and it preserves source provenance. Gemini turns those sources into a plain-language procedure brief: whether a formal review, appeal, complaint, reconsideration, or response route could be verified; where it starts; what deadline is actually supported; which evidence is required or useful; and which parts remain uncertain. If a formal route cannot be responsibly verified, Recourse says so plainly instead of inventing an appeal process. Research is cached for seven days to reduce repeated work and protect the free-tier budget.

Recourse then analyzes the evidence as a connected case rather than treating files as a pile of attachments. It identifies facts that directly address the stated reason, relevant dates, entities, amounts and references, useful documents, missing evidence, contradictions, and a bounded chronology. It can use local extraction for ordinary text and documents and Gemini multimodal understanding for images and scanned pages. If two documents show different dates, it surfaces the discrepancy and asks whether the difference has an explanation; it does not silently choose whichever date makes the response stronger. If an invoice proves a supplier relationship but does not prove authorization, it distinguishes those claims. If the institution requests a document the user cannot obtain, Recourse keeps the gap visible and helps the user consider truthful alternatives. The result is a readiness state that is legible to a stressed person: Needs information, Building your case, Needs evidence, or Ready—not a misleading confidence percentage.

When the case is ready, Recourse gives the user control over the next form of help. The user can generate a grounded email with a subject, factual body, suggested attachments, references, and unresolved facts; generate a professional formal letter that can be previewed, copied, and downloaded as a PDF; or open Ask Recourse for case-aware intelligence. Ask Recourse is especially useful for portal questions such as “Why should this decision be reconsidered?”, “What document should I attach?”, or “How should I describe what changed?” The answer is composed from the current decision, research, evidence facts, clarifications, contradictions, timeline, prior submission, and previous responses. If the case does not contain the fact needed to answer, the agent says that explicitly and asks the user for it. It never turns a guess into a first-person statement on the user’s behalf.

The most important trust feature is the boundary around external action. Recourse prepares and assists, but the user performs the irreversible step. Recourse never sends email, submits a portal or form, clicks a third-party workflow, calls an institution, monitors an external system, or claims that an outside action succeeded. After acting externally, the user selects “I’ve submitted” and records the method, date, optional reference number, and whether they used the Recourse draft unchanged, changed it, or submitted something different. If the draft was changed, the user can paste or upload what was actually submitted. Recourse then preserves that actual submission as the source of truth for future reasoning rather than pretending the first generated draft was sent.

The case continues when the institution responds. The user returns and selects “I received a response,” then pastes or uploads the new message. Recourse compares the response with the original decision, the exact submitted version, relevant evidence, current procedural research, and prior case history. It extracts the outcome, newly stated reason, issues addressed, issues left unanswered, new evidence requests, changed institutional reasoning, and the next legitimate user-controlled route. The user can then draft again, generate another letter, ask a follow-up question, or close the case. This makes Recourse a durable multi-step agent for a real case, not a one-shot content generator that forgets what happened after its first answer.

The agent’s strategy is a bounded loop: observe → understand → ask → research → verify → analyze → prepare → checkpoint → continue. The next operation is selected from the current case state and the remaining unknowns. The MVP uses a small number of inspectable operations—understand case, extract evidence, extract procedure, analyze case, answer case question, draft email, draft formal letter, and analyze response—rather than hiding simple logic inside an opaque swarm. Gemini handles multimodal interpretation and structured reasoning. Tavily provides current external procedure material. MongoDB persists the case, evidence metadata, research, drafts, submission history, and response history. Cloudinary preserves original evidence through backend-controlled uploads. Structured AI responses are validated with Zod before they can influence the case state or appear as a trusted result.

Recourse is intentionally strict about evidence and uncertainty. It keeps three kinds of truth separate: case truth, meaning what the user’s evidence establishes; procedural truth, meaning what current retrieved sources establish; and user choice, meaning what the person decides to do. Documents and web pages are treated as untrusted data rather than instructions. Generated communication is a derived artifact, never evidence. Unsupported facts remain unknown. Conflicting procedure sources are ranked by authority, specificity, jurisdiction, and recency; when the conflict is too severe, the procedure remains unverified. The system can be helpful without manufacturing certainty, and it can be persuasive without becoming deceptive.

The competitive advantage is the combination of breadth, grounding, and continuity. Breadth comes from modeling the universal decision–evidence–procedure problem instead of building brittle adapters for a few platforms. Grounding comes from multimodal evidence analysis, source-ranked live research, provenance, explicit gaps, contradiction detection, and schema-validated outputs. Continuity comes from the actual-submission checkpoint and response comparison, which lets the agent reason from what the institution really received and how the institution’s explanation changed. Together, these features address the full procedural journey: understand first, find the current route, build the record, prepare a truthful response, preserve the external reality, and continue.

The product is useful across consumer advocacy, education, employment, public services, government benefits, finance, insurance, housing, immigration, telecom, marketplaces, creator platforms, and unfamiliar institutional decisions without requiring a domain to be preconfigured. A student can bring a scholarship termination, a seller can bring a marketplace suspension, an applicant can bring a refusal, a tenant can bring a housing decision, a worker can bring a disciplinary notice, and a small business can bring an account restriction. These are examples of the abstraction, not hardcoded workflows. The same agent asks: what happened, what can be established, what process applies, what is missing, what can be said truthfully, what was actually submitted, and what changed next?

This is agentic in the meaningful product sense: it interprets, plans bounded tool calls, retrieves current information, reasons over multimodal evidence, detects gaps, asks for human input when necessary, generates useful artifacts, persists state, and resumes after the world changes. It is not “autonomous” in the dangerous sense of taking an irreversible external action without approval. The user remains the decision-maker while Recourse supplies the procedural clarity and case memory that individuals normally lack.

Recourse’s core promise is simple: when a consequential decision makes the next step unclear, the agent helps a person build a truer case, find the best-supported path, prepare something they can stand behind, and keep going when the institution replies. It does not promise to win every case. It makes the user less dependent on opaque process, less likely to miss relevant evidence, less likely to repeat an unsupported claim, and more capable of making the next decision with context.

name: RAKE
description:
RAKE is an onchain market-forensics agent for Base. Existing token tools tell you what the price
did. RAKE answers the question a trader actually has before buying: when money entered this token,
who got paid when it came back out?

Paste any Base token. A deterministic engine reads every real Swap event in a bounded window (1h,
4h, 24h) straight from Base logs and rebuilds the market. It resolves the pool across Uniswap v2,
v3 and v4, Aerodrome and PancakeSwap - v4 pools are 32-byte ids inside the PoolManager singleton,
so orientation is verified empirically against the pair price rather than assumed. Every sell is
attributed to the human behind it: for ERC-4337 bundles that means the UserOp sender, never the
bundler that submitted it, and never the router. Each swap is priced in USD from its own quote leg
at the hour it executed, not from a spot price applied afterwards.

Sellers are then classified by mechanical rules: first-block (traded in the first 50 swaps after
the pool existed), deployer-funded (first inbound transfer ever came from the initial-LP or a
first-block wallet), cluster (sold alongside sellers sharing one low-degree first funder - one
operator, many hands), lp, and repeat (also sold the previous window). The rake is the share of the
window's inflow that left through those cohorts. Clusters whose shared funder turns out to be an
exchange, bridge or wallet infrastructure are shown and explicitly NOT counted, so ordinary users
are never smeared. House means behaviour matching published rules, never claimed identity.

Only then does a model appear, and it cannot produce a single number - it reads the finished
evidence, may spend a bounded budget of funding lookups, and writes the diagnosis. Thin windows
read TOO THIN, unreadable pools UNPRICEABLE. Nothing is estimated.

Five interfaces, all live: the web receipt (shareable URL, live trace); @basedrakebot on Telegram,
which guards any token and alerts the moment extraction crosses your threshold, running serverless
around the clock; a free SSE API; and an x402 deep pass where another agent pays $0.05 USDC on Base
and receives the full forensic receipt with two-hop funding graphs - no account, no API key.

It keeps running after this submission. Every hour the agent rakes trending Base tokens and commits
each event to a public GitHub log: 80 events across 16 tokens so far. Twelve hours later it audits
itself. That audit currently says its own high-rake signal did NOT precede drawdowns more often
than baseline (0% of 15 high-rake windows fell 30% within 12h, against a 14% baseline). We publish
that anyway, at headline size, because a measurement you cannot audit is an opinion. RAKE measures
extraction, not price - and says so.

name: Verdict
description:
Verdict is an autonomous growth investigator for startups and software agents.

Give Verdict a public startup URL and it investigates the actual product before reaching a judgment. It discovers relevant same-site pages, selects and acquires useful evidence, evaluates coverage across seven growth dimensions, and stops when it has enough evidence or reaches its investigation budget.

The seven dimensions are Positioning & ICP, Messaging & Copy, Website & UX, Conversion Triggers, Trust & Social Proof, Defensibility / Competition, and Growth Foundation.

Only accepted evidence can influence the final report. Models interpret the evidence, but a deterministic scoring engine is the final aggregation authority. Verdict exposes one numerical result: the Growth Readiness Score from 0–100.

The output goes beyond a score. Verdict identifies the primary growth bottleneck, the highest-leverage opportunity, the strongest and weakest areas, and an ordered set of priorities, with supporting source evidence.

The completed audit also remains queryable. Follow-up questions are grounded in the canonical completed report, so Verdict can explain its conclusions without silently changing its ranking or re-evaluating the company from scratch.

Verdict is also agent-native. Software agents can call POST /api/v2/audit through a public x402 endpoint. A production audit costs $0.50 USDC on Base and returns structured audit results directly to the calling agent.

For human users, Verdict provides three free audits per rolling 24 hours. After that, one $0.50 USDC payment unlocks one additional audit. Verdict stores no customer balance and takes no custody of funds.

Competitive advantage: Verdict is not a prompt wrapper or a generic website grader. It combines autonomous multi-page investigation, evidence admission, deterministic scoring, grounded follow-up intelligence, and an x402 machine-to-machine payment rail in one working product.

name: Ovryth
description:
Ovryth is an AI agent that runs payroll for token communities on Base. It lives in a project's Telegram group, reads every contribution, decides what counts as real work under the project's own rules, and pays members in USDC within minutes. Copied and low-effort posts are refused in public, with a reason. The budget never leaves the project's own Base Account, and an on-chain spend permission caps every move the agent can make.

THE PROBLEM
Token communities run on volunteer work: support answers, translations, guides. Paying for it today means a community manager hand-sending tips from a spreadsheet, or a quest platform that holds the budget. Both get farmed by copy-paste spam the moment money appears, and the second means trusting a platform with the treasury.

HOW IT WORKS
The project signs one weekly USDC spend permission from its Base Account, naming the verified OvrythPayer contract as the only spender. Coinbase's SpendPermissionManager enforces the weekly cap on chain. The project can revoke with one signature and the agent stops at once.

For each message the agent runs: a cheap pre-filter (length, links, duplicates, account age and tenure floors), then an LLM (Groq, Gemini fallback) classifies the message against the room's rules and proposes an amount inside the category range, then a deterministic policy layer applies room and member caps. The policy layer can only lower or zero an amount, never raise it. Recipients come only from a wallet the member linked by DM, never from message text, so prompt injection cannot redirect a payment. The result is one of three actions: pay in one transaction, hold for 72 hours when no wallet is linked, or refuse in public with a fixed reason.

FEATURES
- On-chain weekly budget cap via Coinbase spend permissions; funds stay in the project's own Base Account
- AI contribution scoring against each room's own rules, with a written reason for every decision
- Deterministic policy layer that can only lower payouts: room daily cap, per-member caps, category ranges
- Public refusals for duplicates, copied answers, low-effort posts and brand-new accounts
- Room-wide duplicate detection, edit-after-payment tracking, 72-hour holds for unlinked wallets
- Wallet linking by DM only; payment addresses never come from chat text
- Verified payer contract with no withdraw function and no arbitrary call: it can only run pay()
- Owner console: pause, rules changes, one-signature revoke
- Self-serve onboarding at ovryth.midelabs.xyz/onboard, public proof page and live status page

PROOF ON BASE MAINNET
Live payout in the public demo room: 2 USDC for a real answer (0x70e20c42cdef263888e1d40105a972b83556a327fdd586c42c16eaee1360637b). Capped payout to a member wallet (0xdd81d096bfc7edcccda3a327549e8f14953c0c816b1021f90bf2cbd3fa34635a). Over-cap payout reverted on chain (0x2a0e8147e07e9685d8a03443e86a7f605074d889a9d58361e7cb293d2429436b). Revoke in one signature (0x139943041ac91448f6de842ec9151af6e71fa577a564fc82b202bd81ac6d2c96). OvrythPayer verified on BaseScan (0x485457f86fbf5e2385ae183bd5518c7d965e3999). 5 confirmed payouts and 8 refusals so far. Scorer fixture: 3 real contributions paid in range, 7 spam posts refused including a prompt-injection attempt, 0 wrong payments across 3 full runs. 53 unit tests and 7 Foundry Base fork tests, CI green, open source. Demo video: https://x.com/ovryth/status/2101566323935363441

TRY IT
Join t.me/ovryth_demo_room, DM @Ovryth_bot /wallet with your Base address, reply to a pinned question with real work, and get paid in USDC with a BaseScan link. Post a copy from a second account and watch it get refused in public.

WHO PAYS
Token projects, DAOs and launchpad-backed communities that already pay contributors by hand. Planned model: a monthly fee per room plus a small fee on USDC paid out, and a planned OVRY token for fee discounts. Not live.

ROADMAP
Discord support, multi-token budgets, contributor reputation carried across rooms, external security audit of OvrythPayer, and more EVM chains where smart-account spend permissions exist.

WHY IT'S DIFFERENT
Quest platforms hold the budget and review by hand. Ovryth is an agent end to end: it reads, decides, pays and refuses, while the budget stays in the project's own account under a cap enforced on chain.

BUILDER
Built solo by MystiqueMide (Mide Labs, midelabs.xyz). Also shipped Sellvane (sellvane.midelabs.xyz, public sell caps for team token unlocks on Base) and Holdfill (holdfill.midelabs.xyz, limit orders for pre-IPO tokens on Solana).

name: 0GZK
description:
AI is rapidly becoming the new interface for software. Agents can already search, write code, call APIs, and execute complex workflows. But when an AI agent needs to perform a computation that others can actually trust, we need something stronger than an assertion: we need proof.

Zero-knowledge proofs provide that missing layer of trust. They allow computations to be validated without exposing the underlying private inputs, making ZK increasingly relevant for AI agents operating on sensitive data and performing verifiable computation.

The problem is that ZK infrastructure is still difficult to access. Circom circuits can provide powerful proofs, but developers still need to know how to deploy them, find existing circuits, understand their interfaces, and integrate proof generation and verification into their applications.

This is where 0GZK becomes important. It provides a toolkit for making Circom circuit deployment and usage easier, while creating an ecosystem where published circuits can be discovered and reused. With its MCP and AI-agent integrations, an agent can turn this ecosystem into a natural-language interface: instead of manually searching repositories, reading circuit metadata, and wiring up tooling, developers can simply ask for the circuit they need and use it directly.

Our project builds on this idea by making an AI agent the entry point to the 0GZK ecosystem. The agent can discover relevant published circuits, understand what they prove, help developers select the right circuit, and perform off-chain ZK validation as part of an AI-driven workflow.

The goal is simple: make ZK circuits as discoverable and usable by AI agents as APIs are today.

name: Confam
description: Confam is an AI-powered physical-world verification network that lets agents request real-time information from people on the ground. It dispatches nearby humans to verify places, capture photo/video evidence, and get paid in USDC through Base escrow turning real world observations into reliable, reusable data for both people and AI agents.

name: Delivered
description: Delivered is caller-observed delivery proof for paid x402 endpoints. Every existing quality signal stops at the paywall: registries count settlements, monitors probe the 402 challenge, and nobody checks what a paying caller actually receives. Delivered pays as a real buyer, then checks the response against the output contract the seller itself published, in its live 402 challenge or its registry listing, and records the verdict with on-chain settlement evidence. Measured on Base mainnet: of 29 paid responses checkable against their own seller’s contract, 10 violated it, and two endpoints charged real USDC and delivered nothing. Deterministic checking against the seller’s own words needs no arbiter and no trust in us: every verdict ships with the challenge, the response, and the settlement transaction that proves it.

name: PayTack
description:
PayTack is an autonomous, pay-per-call AI Agent marketplace built natively on Base Mainnet. It eliminates recurring SaaS subscriptions in favor of micro-payments in native USDC via the x402 payment standard and transfer authorizations. PayTack operates a suite of 7 specialized on-chain and analytical agents:

1. Smart Contract Auditor & Proxy Analyzer: Performs semantic and proxy-aware vulnerability audits on verified/unverified contracts on Base.

2. Deep Token & Honeypot Forensics: Inspects liquidity health, FDV, holder distribution, and buy/sell tax mechanics.

3. DeFi Yield Finder: Ranks real-time APYs and calculates impermanent loss risk across Base protocols (Aerodrome, Uniswap V3, Moonwell, Seamless).

4. Algorithmic Trading Strategist: Multi-timeframe trend analysis with technical indicators (RSI, EMA, Bollinger, Order Flow) and execution plans (Entry, SL, TP, Risk-Reward).

5. Wallet Forensics & PnL Profiling: Analyzes trade win-rates and smart-money behavior on Base.

6. Hack Exposure & Approvals Check: Forensically audits wallet approvals and interaction history against known drainers and exploited contracts.

7. Crypto Research & Content Writer: Generates institutional-grade market briefs and structured research threads.

PayTack fuses real-time on-chain RPC data feeds, Basescan V2 smart contract bytecode/storage slot analysis, and live DeFi liquidity pools with Groq hardware-accelerated LLMs. Payment flows are handled seamlessly via EIP-3009 cryptographic permit signatures without requiring ETH for gas.

what sets PayTack Aside:

- Pay-per-Call Utility: No monthly subscriptions or credit cards; users sign micro-payments in USDC directly from their Web3 wallet.

- Orion Reputation Token Integration: Automatically detects on-chain AgentBound soulbound tokens on Base to provide dynamic tier-based fee discounts (up to 40% off).

- Multi-Channel Dispatch: Delivers real-time interactive browser reports alongside instant automated alerts and report pushes via Telegram (@PayTackBot).

- Deep Proxy & Storage Forensics: Resolves EIP-1967 implementation slots and unverified contracts directly on-chain rather than relying on shallow static analyzers.

name: Obelus
description: Obelus is a fact-checking agent for crypto announcements. Paste an X post, a press-release link or the text, or ask "Is $PEPE listed on MEXC?". A model only pulls out the claims, quoting each one exactly. Code then checks each claim against the one source that can confirm it: the exchange's own API (WEEX, BingX, Binance, Bybit, OKX, MEXC), CertiK's project page, the Base blockchain, the partner's own website or DefiLlama. Each claim is marked verified, contradicted or unverified, with a link to its proof. Missing proof is never called false. Every report gets a tamper-proof receipt on Base. It works on the web, in Telegram and through an API.

name: LIVING ALPHA COUNCIL
description: Living Alpha Council is a transparent multi-agent research system that investigates the Base ecosystem using live evidence, adversarial debate, and independent evidence auditing. Five specialized AI agents discover, debate, attack, audit, and adjudicate every research thesis before it can be published.

name: Watchtower
description:
Watchtower is a read-only Base protocol upgrade investigation tool.

A proxy upgrade event only shows that an implementation changed. Watchtower
reconstructs the evidence around that event by verifying the configured
transaction, exact historical proxy state, implementation bytecode, and
protocol-specific identity checks at the relevant Base block.

It then produces a deterministic investigation outcome and a replayable JSON
receipt that anyone can verify in the browser.

The current version supports three configured Base profiles:
Aave V3, Compound III, and ether.fi.

name: CoinOp
description:
CoinOp is a pay-per-use AI thread writer that owns its own wallet and pays its own bills.

What it does: the user picks one of six modes (Hot Take, Educational, Token Analysis, Daily Recap, Chain Comparison, News Breakdown), types a topic, and reads the opening tweet as a free sample. Unlocking the full thread costs $0.10 in USDC on Base. The agent then spends its own money on the job: 1-4 x402 micro-payments to Groq, Serper, CoinGecko and DefiLlama, streamed live as a trace, and returns a ready-to-post X thread plus an itemised receipt of what each call cost on-chain.

name: Proof of Delivery
description:
Proof of Delivery is an autonomous agent that buys things on Base and refuses to be cheated doing it. It screens the counterparty before it signs, verifies the settlement transaction on Base after it pays, verifies that the response is actually what was quoted, and turns every outcome into hash-chained seller reputation that anyone can recompute from the published log. It has made six real purchases from four independent third-party sellers on Base mainnet, refused a seventh before a signature existed, and anchored the resulting ledger on chain — every one of those facts re-checkable against Base in a single command.

## The problem

x402 turns an HTTP request into a purchase: a server answers 402 Payment Required with a price, the buying agent signs a USDC transferWithAuthorization (EIP-3009) into a header, the server settles it on Base and serves the resource. One round trip, no account, no invoice. The protocol specifies how the money moves and says nothing about whether the buyer got anything for it. Three gaps follow, all on the buyer's side. Nobody screens the counterparty: payTo is an arbitrary address in a JSON body, and an agent will sign an authorization to whatever a server puts in front of it. Nobody checks the settlement: the PAYMENT-RESPONSE header carrying the transaction hash and success: true is written by the same party that took the money, which makes it a claim, not a receipt. Nobody checks the delivery: a 200 OK whose body is an apology is, protocol-wise, a completed purchase.

These are documented, not hypothetical. The @x402/next README states that its paymentProxy "will charge clients for failed API responses", and that a route-pattern typo means "the handler runs without payment protection". We checked the sharper version of that claim before repeating it: @x402/express 2.24.0 and legacy x402-express 1.2.0 both contain "If the response from the protected route is >= 400, do not settle payment", so the charge-on-failure hazard is specific to the Next.js proxy mode. What survives is the structural point: a buyer can be billed for a response it never got, a seller can give away paid content, and neither can detect its own case from its own side.

## What it does

Every purchase runs through eight stages, and the one that matters is the one that stops it: quote, counterparty, policy gate, sign, settle, verify settlement, verify delivery, receipt. The policy gate is thirteen named rules — network, asset, scheme, per-call cap, budget, denylist, counterparty risk, resource-host binding, quote staleness, price stability, nonce replay, seller reputation floor, rate limit — and every applicable one must pass before a signature exists. A rule that could not be evaluated is a denial, not a pass, because an unavailable check is not a clean check. Refusals are rendered with the numbers compared, in a sentence a person can read: "quoted 1000 (0.001 USDC) exceeds the 500 per-call cap". Settlement verification pulls the seller's claimed transaction from Base and checks six things: it exists, it succeeded, the asset is USDC, the amount is exact, the recipient is the quoted payTo, the payer is us. An overpayment fails as loudly as an underpayment. Delivery verification checks the response against what the challenge advertised — status, emptiness, media type, parsability, latency, and the 200-that-is-really-an-error case. A model may adjudicate content, but it is clamped in code so it can only lower a verdict, never raise one, and if it is unavailable the deterministic verdict stands and the receipt says so. No score, amount, risk number or settlement verdict in this product comes from a model.

## Reputation is earned, never declared

Each outcome becomes a hash-chained receipt, and a seller's score is a pure function of that ledger, recomputable by anyone from the published log — derivedFrom names the exact receipt hashes behind every score. One paid_settlement_unverified caps a seller at 1500 out of 10000 regardless of history, because a counterparty that misreports settlement has poisoned its own evidence. A seller with fewer than three settled interactions stays Unrated rather than being flattered by a small sample. Refusing to pay is never held against a seller: those receipts are counted but never move a delivery score, because they describe our policy, not their behaviour. A partial delivery is weighted strictly between a clean one and none at all — half credit in the rate and a real penalty — because a seller that ships eight of ten promised fields is not the same as one that ships an apology. A hash chain cannot detect truncation at the tail, so the head is anchored on Base: the chain protects the middle, the anchor protects the end.

## Both sides of the market

Proof of Delivery is a buyer and a seller. As a buyer it pays real x402 endpoints on Base mainnet. As a seller it exposes its own reputation data behind its own x402 gate: a complete seller implementation with EIP-712 signature recovery, exact-amount enforcement, authorization-nonce replay protection checked against USDC's own authorizationState before every broadcast, on-chain settlement, and reputation-based pricing that drops the quote from $0.02 to $0.005 for an attested buyer and fails closed with HTTP 400 on a tampered or expired attestation rather than silently charging full price. It also exposes a public, keyless, stateless read-only report endpoint that answers a live x402 URL in under three seconds, which is the only shape the Orion Agent Store can invoke; one of twenty listed agents currently has one.

## Where Orion's primitives sit in this

They are the trust anchor, not a logo. The oracle address is read from the AgentBound ERC-5192 registry on Base rather than from Orion's API, so a compromised or absent host cannot change who is trusted to sign reputation. That stopped being theoretical on 2 September, when orionagents.org went down for a systemwide upgrade and served a placeholder on every path including /api: our trust anchor kept working and reported the outage as an outage, distinguishing "the host could not be reached" from "the host disagrees" — because collapsing those two would let a downed server read as a finding, or worse, as the claim that an agent has no reputation. @pod/orion is an open, clean-room implementation of the attestation verifier that Orion's own documentation says is not published to npm: the same nine-line EIP-191 message, rebuilt from the fields and compared byte-for-byte before any signature is recovered. And the receipts this agent produces are exactly the kind of observed performance an AgentBound weekly attestation is specified to consume, expressed in Orion's own format.

## Proof, checkable in one command with no wallet

Ten on-chain claims live in data/claims.json and re-verify against a public Base RPC with node scripts/verify-onchain.mjs — no install, no credentials, exits non-zero on the first claim that fails. All ten hold: six settlement transactions from real purchases, the ledger anchor, the AgentBound bytecode, the oracle read, and the revert proving the registry is empty. We also graded Orion's production x402 gateway with our own adversarial suite, read-only and sending no payment: grade A, eight of eight probes failing closed, and all five forged attestations refused with a distinct reason each — including a genuine EIP-191 signature over a byte-perfect message, self-signed by a freshly generated key claiming Platinum and a score of 9900, which came back "signature does not recover to the Orion oracle address". Reproduce it with pnpm conformance. And we swept the live Base x402 population on 2 September: 1,617 hosts, one unpaid GET each, nothing signed — 1,031 correctly gated, 122 serving a malformed challenge, 8 dead, 4 serving listed-as-paid content with no payment challenge at all, and 34 advertising Stripe's MPP rail on the same 402 as x402. We publish 1,031 as a floor rather than an estimate, because 674 endpoints declare a non-GET method and their gate is invisible to a GET sweep; we deliberately did not run a POST sweep, because sending a write-shaped verb to hundreds of third-party production endpoints to enlarge our own coverage figure is not a trade this project makes. The finding worth citing from that sweep: 99.9% of gated endpoints bind their price to a resource, but only 28.7% do it on the offer itself and 3.3% publish the binding only on the transport a client did not select — so any x402 client reading a single transport misjudges roughly one Base seller in thirty, in the seller's disfavour. The suite is 1,263 tests and runs offline with no credentials, including a property test over 20,000 generated inputs asserting no payment is ever approved unless every rule passed, and another asserting the content model can never raise a delivery verdict.

## What we do not claim, and what we got wrong

CLAIMS.md tags every public statement by evidence tier and lists what we deliberately do not claim; MOCKS.md draws the exact line between live calls and fixtures. The honest headline limit: no Orion AgentBound attestation has been verified end-to-end against a real minted token, because the registry has zero mints — ownerOf(1) reverts, and that revert is one of the ten verified claims. Three corrections we made against ourselves are worth stating, because each was caught by our own instruments and each moved a number in someone else's favour. Running the census with the same parser we pay with revealed that our client mis-read the 79.6% of Base challenges that arrive header-only with an empty body, which would have made us refuse most of the market and score it malformed. Re-probing sixty flagged endpoints with full bodies showed the largest cause of "header/body mismatch" was offers serialized in a different order on each transport — same money, same recipient — and splitting material from cosmetic dropped our malformed count from 251 to 121; publishing the first number would have overstated seller defects roughly fivefold. And a live purchase was refused against an honest seller for "declaring no resource URL" when it declares one exactly where the v2 spec puts it, at the challenge level; we reset the ledger rather than publish a receipt blaming a third party for our bug.

name: shanks
description: Metron lets AI agents negotiate real financial data prices instead of paying flat, expensive rates like Bloomberg or Glassnode. Agents propose a price, the seller accepts or counters and payment settles instantly via x402 on Base. it's the negotiation and settlement layer for cheap, machine-to-machine data purchases, live on Base mainnet with real proven transactions.

name: Sellvane
description:
Sellvane is an AI agent that sells a crypto team's unlocked tokens under a public daily cap enforced on Base, and only when the pool can take the sale.

THE PROBLEM
Vesting schedules say when team tokens unlock, not how fast they get sold. On unlock day holders can't see how much the team is allowed to sell, so they sell first and the price falls. Launchpads and exchanges carry the reputational cost.

HOW IT WORKS
The team signs one Coinbase spend permission from its Base Account: at most N tokens per 24 hours, spendable only by the verified SellvaneSeller contract. Coinbase's SpendPermissionManager enforces the cap on chain, so Sellvane cannot sell above it. We tested it: Base rejected a sale one token over the cap (tx 0xbe249cc824b778d0d740786eb7e0e6342449f9b897ed2145a4d8d500354e8f20). The team can revoke at any time, which stops every future sale.

Every 10 minutes the agent reads the cap, the Uniswap v3 pool and the time to reset. Code quotes a ladder of sale sizes on QuoterV2 and finds the largest slice under the team's price impact limit (default 1%). An LLM (Groq, gpt-oss-120b) picks SELL 25, 50, 75 or 100% of that slice, or WAIT, with a one-line reason. Invalid output becomes WAIT. Every sale is simulated first, carries an on-chain price floor, and the ETH returns to the team account in the same transaction.

FEATURES
- Public daily sell cap enforced on chain by Coinbase spend permissions
- AI agent that sizes and times sales inside the cap, with a written reason for every move
- Price impact limit per sale, set by the team (0.5%, 1% or 2%)
- Bypass watch: any transfer out of the team account that is not a Sellvane sale is flagged publicly
- Live cap page per token, readable by anyone, every number read from Base
- Launchpad view: one table of every capped token
- Self-serve setup: any team checks its token, picks a cap and previews sales before signing
- Telegram bot with the same data: /cap, /moves, /bypass, /pool, /check
- Non-custodial: tokens stay in the team account until each sale, and the team can revoke at any time
- Rate limits in code: 30-minute cooldown, 12 sales a day, gas floor

PROOF ON BASE MAINNET
5,000,000 token daily cap on our test token. 11 agent sales so far, highest price impact 0.72%. 1 over-cap sale rejected by Base. 0 transfers outside the cap. SellvaneSeller verified on BaseScan (0x719a235Be27F0b7B7F82775aFBEA6a2dE6264fe6). 11 Foundry fork tests and 30 unit tests, CI green, open source. Demo video: https://youtu.be/rRFIAhth9Ak

WHO PAYS
Launchpads are the buyer: they can require a Sellvane cap as a listing condition and show holders a table of capped tokens. Planned model: a per-token fee for launchpads plus a small fee on agent-executed sales. Planned token: VANE, for fee discounts and launchpad staking. Not live.

ROADMAP
Aerodrome and Uniswap v4 pools, multisig treasuries through smart-account permissions, more EVM chains with smart-account spend permissions, and a public API for launchpads and exchanges.

WHY IT'S DIFFERENT
TWAP tools split one order. Sellvane gives holders a standing public limit, enforced by Base, with an agent that sells inside it and a public flag for anything that goes around it.

BUILDER
Built solo by MystiqueMide (Mide Labs, midelabs.xyz), a full-stack and smart contract builder who ships live products for hackathons: Holdfill (non-custodial limit orders for pre-IPO tokens on Solana, holdfill.midelabs.xyz) and Ovryth (ovryth.midelabs.xyz)—a 3x hackathon winner.

name: Shamar
description:
An agent you can hand a recurring bill to.

Ask people what they spend on subscriptions and they say around $86 a month. The real figure is $219. Seven in ten have been charged for a free trial they meant to cancel, and $15.5 billion a year goes to apps nobody opens.

None of that is forgetfulness. Renewing requires nothing. Cancelling requires a login, a retention screen and sometimes a phone call, and when the FTC tried to force click-to-cancel in 2025 the rule was struck down. The friction is the business model, and it is now legally protected.

You already know you should audit this. You have known for months. The reason you have not is that cancelling the wrong thing takes a design library with it, or cuts off a teammate, or gives up a price the service stopped offering, and no list of charges tells you which is which.

SHAMAR makes the call. It reads your receipts, weighs what cancelling costs against what it saves, asks you three times, and acts if you never answer.

name: BaseScout
description: BaseScout is an autonomous AI DeFi research analyst built for the Base network. It investigates any Base token by fetching live market data (price, liquidity, volume, etc.) and on-chain facts directly from the Base RPC. It then runs a deterministic risk engine to evaluate liquidity depth, rug surface, and wash-trading tells. Finally, Claude analyzes these verifiable on-chain facts to produce an honest, hype-free research brief. Every claim made by BaseScout traces back to a real tool call, making it a reliable tool for traders to DYOR before investing.

name: ShowingKit
description:
ShowingKit reads a listing before you walk in, builds a timed shot list for the exact room that usually hides the lie, then diffs your visit photos against the listing and either stamps "Walk", " Negotiate" or  "Offer" with a same-day ask and three texts. 

The strategy is not “inspect the house.” It is own the twenty-minute gap where renters and first-time buyers actually decide. 

The advantage is when it acts, and what it outputs.

Most tools either chat about apartments or do a full inspection. 

ShowingKit does neither. It sits in the twenty minutes you actually get: 

1. listing language in, 

2. timed shots during, 

3. stamp and texts out before you leave the curb.

That gives you three things competitors usually miss:

1. Proof, not vibes. The agent provides a listing-claim vs a visit-photo table. “Flex 2BR” against a windowless wall. “New kitchen” against the toe-kick they cropped.

2. Your dealbreakers:  You set what fails the unit. A Legal bedroom, in-unit laundry, no leaks, etc. The agent's brief scores against that, along with the city’s rules (a windowless “flex” room in New York is not the same problem as damp in London).

name: Sovereign
description: Sovereign  is a Telegram-native AI agent for real service businesses. Owners configure niche, services, price bounds, a Base mainnet USDC wallet, and alerts once; the agent then runs the full commercial loop—dynamic intake, affordable quotes within owner rules, professional proposal PDFs, payment instructions, and on-chain verification of USDC transfers on Base. Only a successful chain check marks a job paid; the LLM never confirms money. Clients receive receipts and invoices automatically; owners manage orders, stats, delivery, and multi-owner isolation via invite slugs. It pairs AI judgment with deterministic settlement so studios can operate commercially in chat without screenshot payments or spreadsheet chaos.

name: Obsign Sentinel
description: Obsign Sentinel is an AI-assisted verification agent that checks credentials and supporting evidence before a decision is made. It creates an auditable receipt that others can independently verify, helping teams and agents avoid relying on screenshots, private databases, or unverified claims.

name: Kryptic check
description: Kryptic Check is a Web3 claim verification agent that tests crypto claims against retrieved evidence. Users can provide a claim and source URL or use open search. It returns Supported, Partially Supported, Contradicted, or Unverified, with reasoning and evidence links. It does not treat missing evidence as proof and does not provide financial advice.

name: Drift-d
description:
WHAT IT DOES

Drift-d watches two independent signals for a Base token and reports the hours they stop agreeing. Attention and money move at different speeds: a token gets loud before volume shows up, or volume moves while nobody is talking. Neither number means much on its own. The information is in the gap between them, and that gap is the only thing this agent reports.

STRATEGY

Every hour it pulls social momentum (interactions across X, Reddit, YouTube and TikTok) and onchain momentum (volume in that token's own Base pool, not aggregate cross-venue volume). Each side is ranked against its own history, then subtracted. The score is fully deterministic — no model touches it. Claude reads the result and explains which of four kinds of gap it is, but never computes the number. Thin pools get a volume floor set per pool rather than in dollars, so a ratio between two near-zero hours cannot publish a confident reading. When an event fires, a direct Base RPC call reads the pool contract's live reserves to cross-check the aggregator. Output is 125 events across 12 Base tokens, committed hourly to a public file with timestamps.

COMPETITIVE EDGE

It checks itself, and publishes the result even when the result is bad. Drift-d went back over every event it has ever produced and measured whether the lagging series actually followed: 27.5% of the time, against a 38.5% base rate for any random hour. Its own signal performs worse than chance, and that number is printed on the homepage at headline size rather than buried. Every other entry claims its agent works. This one shows the receipt in both directions, which is the only version of that claim a judge can verify.

name: ScamLens
description:
ScamLens AI is an autonomous AI-powered security investigator built to help people identify scams and risky crypto projects before they interact with them.

The idea comes from a simple problem: crypto moves fast, but verifying what you are interacting with is still too difficult. A user might come across a token on Base, receive a wallet address, discover a new project on X, or be sent to an unfamiliar website. Determining whether it is legitimate can require checking multiple sources, reading contract code, examining wallet activity, researching the team, and looking for suspicious patterns.

ScamLens AI brings that investigation into one place.

Instead of simply telling users whether something is "safe" or "a scam," ScamLens acts like a digital forensic investigator. A user can provide a wallet address, smart-contract address, website, or X profile, and the agent gathers relevant evidence, analyzes different risk signals, and produces an understandable investigation report.

For a Base-based token or wallet, for example, ScamLens can examine on-chain activity, contract permissions, ownership, liquidity behavior, transaction patterns, and other available signals, while also combining off-chain information such as website and social credibility.

The result is a Trust Score, Scam Probability, Risk Level, and AI-generated explanation showing why the system reached its conclusion.

Why ScamLens AI is being built

ScamLens is built because security shouldn't require everyone to become a blockchain investigator.

New users often don't know what a malicious contract looks like. Even experienced users can miss warning signs when dealing with hundreds of new tokens, wallets, and projects appearing every day.

ScamLens aims to reduce that gap by turning complicated security research into a simple workflow:

Paste → Investigate → Understand → Decide.

Its focus on Base makes it particularly useful within a rapidly growing on-chain ecosystem, where users need tools that can help them make more informed decisions without manually jumping between explorers, contract scanners, websites, social platforms, and other research tools.

Ultimately, ScamLens AI isn't designed to replace human judgment. It's designed to give users the evidence they need before they make a decision.

The mission is simple: make on-chain safety understandable, accessible, and proactive.

Agents build a fully quoted, unsigned payout plan (fees, gas, slippage) on Base and Arc that a wallet owner reviews and authorizes step-by-step from their own wallet. Competitive advantage: deterministic in-pool pricing, MCP-native plumbing, and it works end-to-end today.

name: ShadowDetective
description: ShadowDetective is an autonomous on-chain cyber forensics and security intelligence agent built for Base mainnet.Strategy:The agent combines deterministic EVM bytecode inspection with multi-role AI reasoning (Detective, Prosecutor, Defender) to audit smart contracts, token pools, and suspect wallets in real-time. It maps entity relationship topologies (deployers, AMM pairs, mixers like Tornado Cash) onto an interactive visual Crime Board and reconstructs capital funding ancestry.Competitive Advantage:Unlike generic AI tools that hallucinate accusations, ShadowDetective enforces an "Evidence First, Narrative Second" architecture. Every threat score is mathematically tied to deterministic on-chain indicators (unverified proxies, hidden mint selectors, liquidity drain vectors, and blacklist traps) while dynamically generating unique behavioral fingerprints and archetypes for personal wallets.

name: OrionX
description:
What It Does:
OrionX Sentinel is a non-custodial, autonomous DeFi security sentinel and capital co-pilot built natively for Base Mainnet. Operating 24/7 with zero simulated data, it continuously monitors user wallets to defend against silent liquidation cascades, identify and revoke risky ERC-20 smart contract allowances , mathematically optimize capital allocation across top Base yield pools, and track ecosystem incentive qualifications. OrionX pairs an interactive web dashboard with an autonomous, always-on background Telegram daemon (@OrionXSentinelBot) that dispatches real-time proactive push alerts whenever health factors fall below safety thresholds ($HF < 1.50$) or critical contract upgrades occur.

Strategy:
OrionX employs a Risk-First Solvency & Net-Gain Yield Strategy. It unifies multi-protocol telemetry across Moonwell, Compound III, Aave V3, and Seamless into an aggregate health factor, automatically computing defensive debt repayment deltas before liquidations hit. Simultaneously, its yield engine runs net-profit routing ($\text{Target APY} - \text{Current APY} - \text{Gas Cost} - \text{Slippage}$) to safely capture real yield while maintaining maximum on-chain solvency and permission security.

Competitive Advantage:

- 100% Genuine On-Chain Telemetry (Zero Simulated Data): Direct multi-RPC fallback querying live Base contracts, allowances, and position snapshots.

- Multi-Protocol Solvency Shield: Unified health-factor aggregation and instant protective repayment calculation across all major Base lending markets.

- 24/7 Background Sentinel Daemon: Proactive automated monitoring and instant Telegram push alerts even when the user is offline.

- Deep 6-Dimensional AI Protocol Vetting: Instant contract auditing covering proxy slots, oracle manipulation vectors, multisig thresholds, and bad debt exposure.

- Complete Non-Custodial Architecture: Direct Wagmi/Viem smart contract execution where user funds and signing keys always remain strictly under user custody.

name: VETTE
description:
VETTE is the agent that vets agents. Give it any agent's website or wallet and
it reads what the agent promised, checks what it actually did on Base, and rules
on whether the behavior matches the promise: COMPLIANT, DEVIATED, DANGEROUS, or
UNVERIFIABLE — with a score and a public receipt. Every verdict carries its
evidence.

The deterministic engine runs first and decides what is true: it fetches the
agent's own copy, extracts its stated promises, then reads the wallet's real
history — transactions, token transfers, owner-scoped approval events, and live
allowances probed onchain. A rule engine scores deviation and wallet safety.
It never invents evidence. If a wallet is empty or unpublished, the verdict is
UNVERIFIABLE — not flattering, and not fiction.

Then Vette acts. The Alibi rebuilds any wallet's money-trail from Base — every
inflow, every outflow, where each coin went next — and hands back the receipts
(THE MONEY CAME HOME / THE MONEY LEFT / TRAIL TOO SHALLOW). Motive is a matter
for humans; the trail is a matter of receipts. And connect your wallet and every
dangerous approval becomes a one-click kill switch: approve(spender, 0),
preflight-simulated onchain before any signature, confirmed with the tx hash on
screen. Every other entry describes problems. Vette ends them.

Vette also vets the whole field: it pulls the hackathon's own entry API, puts
every registered wallet and builder claim under the same lens, and re-checks
them daily at 06:00 UTC with every run committed to a public GitHub log. Its
first live catch: a leading entry whose published wallet is actually a token
contract.

name: Verdict
description: Verdict is a pre-action security gate for autonomous AI agents. Before an agent executes a sensitive action (transfers, swaps, contract interactions), Verdict verifies its cryptographic identity, policy limits, and anomaly signals to render an instant verdict: ALLOW (executes on-chain on Base), REVIEW (escalates for human approval), or REJECT (genuinely blocks execution before a transaction can be produced).

name: AEGIS
description: Aegis is an autonomous token risk intelligence and security agent designed to protect users and listing teams from scams, rug pulls, and malicious smart contracts on Base. It executes deterministic on-chain security checks evaluating liquidity locks, holder concentration, contract ownership, and trading restrictions within seconds. Built with Gemini integration, Aegis transforms complex smart contract code and raw on-chain data into institutional grade listing decisions and risk briefs.

name: Sidik
description:
Sidik proves what a Base ERC-20 does to a buyer by doing it, rather than inferring risk from bytecode. Given an address, it forks Base mainnet at a pinned block with anvil and executes six probes as real transactions: it buys and sells (honeypot), measures buy, sell and transfer separately and again a day later in fork time (hidden fee), grants an allowance and drains it (approval drain), classifies the LP holder and impersonates it to pull the pool (LP rug), compares pool pricing against BingX and Gate (cross-venue), and impersonates the privileged address to pull every ownership switch it can find, then makes the identical sell again (owner trap). Every verdict is decided by deterministic code reading the result of a mined transaction. The model orders the probes and writes the prose; a numeric guard rejects any figure that does not appear verbatim in the run data, so it cannot invent a verdict, a hash or a number.

Paste any Base address and it will fork the chain and execute the probes while you watch, in about thirty seconds; the 207 already recorded answer instantly instead. Hosting that meant giving up on container hosts — every one of them wanted a card or a paid tier — and putting Foundry inside a serverless function, which is the difference between an agent you can read about and one you can point at your own token.

The same run is a pre-listing check. Can it be sold, does the trade get skimmed, can the pool be emptied, can one address close the exit — those are the questions an exchange or a launchpad answers before a token goes live, and they are the four this executes rather than estimates. It never scores a token or says whether to list it; it reports what happened when it tried.

The catalogue is 207 Base addresses and 1,843 fork transactions. 68 fail at least one probe: 37 LP rugs, 25 owner traps, 18 hidden fees, 7 honeypots, 1 drainable wallet. 29 pass everything that applied; 110 return N/A — always reported as "not answered", never as "safe". The largest cause of N/A used to be the LP-rug probe failing to find a V3 position in its own search window; that was our limitation rather than the chain's, and fixing it turned 88 of those rows into statements about the pool.

The finding the project exists for: 203 of the 206 checkable addresses publish verified source code, and so do 59 of the 60 with a finding against them. Sourcify, asked independently, holds 67 exact and 39 partial matches. "Check that the contract is verified" separates almost nothing on Base. The catalogue was also run through GoPlus and honeypot.is, with every disagreement published in both directions: on buy tax GoPlus matched the executed figure on 185 of 185 addresses, and on whether a privileged address can still stop a holder from leaving it agreed on 12 of 42. 25 tokens have such an address, and 9 of them — including USDC, EURC, cbBTC and cbETH — pass every other probe. 17 of the 25 are proxy admins replacing the implementation. That is a proof of capability, not an accusation or a prediction, and the interface says so on the page.

What it refuses to do is as deliberate as what it does. Fork transactions are never linked to a block explorer, because they were never broadcast. An address with no recorded run returns an error, never a clean bill of health. A probe with no mechanism to test returns N/A rather than PASS. The public site replays the recorded catalogue by default, because a replay answers instantly and cannot be rate-limited, and executes a fresh run on request. The recorded runs are genuine output of the engine in this repository, frozen, and `pnpm --filter @sidik/engine reproduce <address>` re-forks Base at the same block with your own RPC and diffs the result against what is published. It runs in CI on every push.

Reproducibility is the claim it stakes everything on, so it is stated as a number rather than a promise: `reproduce --sample 3` re-forked Base at the same block and returned 9 verdicts reproduced, 0 differed. All three findings, each with its method and the rows behind it, are at /findings — including the one comparison Sidik loses.

Every surface is machine-readable: JSON per address and for the catalogue, an OpenAPI 3.1 schema, an llms.txt, provenance on every body (recording date, engine commit, sha256 of the catalogue), and an MCP server over Streamable HTTP exposing sidik_token, sidik_catalogue and sidik_run, so an agent asked "is this token safe?" can call a fork execution instead of a scanner.

name: Avelune
description:
Avelune is a personal crypto trading agent that learns how each trader makes decisions from real TAKE and PASS calibration examples. It autonomously watches the trader's configured markets around the clock then either sends a signal, paper trades, request approvals or execute  through Binance spot testnet.
unlike other AI signal tools;  Avelune follows the individual trader's own playbook not someone else.
 It follows your playbook, preferences, your risk rules and helps you learn from the results over time.

name: Fork
description:
Fork is a non-custodial risk agent for Moonwell lending on Base. A wallet can look healthy right now and still get wrecked by a governance change that has already been encoded. Fork takes that known change, applies it on a real Base mainnet fork, and asks the protocol contracts whether the wallet is still solvent — before the change hits the live chain.

You paste a Base address (or use a demo wallet). Fork reads the live position, finds supported protocol changes that actually touch that wallet, replays the change on a fork, and returns before/after risk from the contracts. If a rescue is in scope, it only offers repay-debt or add-collateral plans that still pass after the change. You sign on Base. Fork never holds keys and never sends a transaction.

Strategy: the model proposes, the EVM proves. Groq may pick analysis tools and explain the trace. It cannot invent balances, declare solvency, or build arbitrary transactions. No mocked chain data. Unknown protocol behavior fails closed.

Advantage over typical Base risk dashboards: they score the wallet as it is. Fork scores the wallet after a known protocol future. Proofs are receipts from a real fork, not a chatbot opinion. V1 is Moonwell Core on Base, starting with a real collateral-factor change (proposal 176). Other protocols and server-side sends are out of scope for now.

name: Rigel
description:
Rigel is an autonomous wallet diagnostics agent for Base. A deterministic engine reads any address and measures what is structurally wrong with the portfolio: concentration, dry powder, long tail weight, unpriced and spam positions, drawdown, dormancy, and more, then scores it out of 100.

The agent reads that output and decides for itself what the first pass missed. It scans other chains when a concentration reading looks like a single chain artifact, and pulls token approvals when the wallet holds enough to be worth draining.

Everything it finds is re scored by the same engine, so the health score moves based on evidence rather than opinion.

On jesse.base.eth, the baseline reads 85/100. The agent chose to check approvals, found $1,293 reachable through 19 live approvals, and the score fell to 67.

The model chooses where to look and writes the diagnosis. It never produces a number. Every figure traces back to a real API call, and the full sequence of decisions streams live in the trace.

Most portfolio tools show you what you hold. Rigel tells you what is wrong with it.

name: AgentTrial
description: AgentTrial is the evidence layer for agent marketplaces. It autonomously turns advertised capabilities into sealed, claim-specific adversarial trials, executes bounded scenarios, scores results using deterministic assertions, and issues signed tamper-evident receipts anyone can verify. Builders get reproducible proof, marketplaces get a reusable vetting primitive, and users can distinguish identity from demonstrated performance. Its live Base-deployed demo requires no account or paid API key and includes head-to-head benchmarking, browser-local Ed25519 verification, and an independently inspectable Base Sepolia EAS anchor.

name: Nemesis
description:
Nemesis is an autonomous crypto incident response agent for compromised wallets. 
Starting with only a wallet address, it discovers and verifies the likely theft transaction, traces stolen funds across subsequent wallets and transactions, detects swaps and cross chain movement, monitors the trail for new activity, and turns verified onchain evidence into an investigation case that can support recovery and escalation. 

Unlike block explorers and one time tracing tools, Nemesis continues the investigation after the initial trace. It combines deterministic blockchain verification with AI interpretation, using Google ADK and Gemini, with Alchemy, Bitquery, GoPlus and Chainabuse for onchain discovery and enrichment. Nemesis currently supports Ethereum and Base, making it directly usable for tracing incidents across the Base ecosystem while preserving the same evidence-first workflow.

name: Arksonus_ai
description:
My AI is a tool that goes beyond this hackathon, a tool that everybody wants to use because it solves a real problem, X spaces are where Alphas are shared the most, but conversations disappear as soon as the space ends Or as soon as X deletes the recording from their database, so I built an Agent that lets you download any X space recording directly as an Mp3 or Mp4 audio that you can play back anytime and anywhere, and my agent is integrated with deepseek to also turn that audio recording into Transcripts that can be stored into a database, so information is never lost, it also helps you finds the best moments from the space so Clippers that use it to clip for their favourite projects and projects also can use it as a soundtrack for documentaries.

That's how good the tech is.

name: Shield
description:
Shield is a safety scanner for Base that judges a wallet by what surrounds it, not just what is inside it. Paste any address and it reads live chain data: history, token approvals, native balance, and the fund flow network two hops up the funding trail.

The problem it solves: burner and bot wallets look clean by their own history. A day-old wallet with five transactions is a blank page to every history-based tool. But every action needs gas, and gas has to come from somewhere. Shield follows the gas.

What Shield measures:

Seed funding trail: two hops up, with funder profiling. In the live demo it detected a gas dispenser that drip-fed 20 fresh wallets with 0.0005 ETH amounts or less, and resolved the dispenser's own funder one hop further up.
Forwarding velocity: median deposit-to-forward time measured from raw blocks. The demo burner pushes deposits back out in about 22 seconds (samples: 30s, 22s, 6s). That is not human speed.
Sweeper detection, taint severity, cluster analysis, token approvals, and live chain state.
Every verdict ships with a receipt: a SHA-256 content digest that recomputes in the browser on the verify page. Change one byte and the hash breaks. The verdict is math, not opinion.

Two honest design choices:

Unattributed verdicts. Shield measures infrastructure shape, it does not dox anyone.
No fake scores. If a read fails, the receipt prints INSUFFICIENT DATA and names the check that did not complete. A made up score is worse than no score, because people make real wallet decisions based on it.
Concrete catch from the live demo on Base mainnet: a one-day-old wallet, five transactions total, near-empty balance. Its own history: clean. Shield's verdict: CAUTION, score 800/1000 capped. Seed funder: gas dispenser, 20 wallets funded. Hop-2 funder resolved. Median forward: 22 seconds. The wallet looked clean. The network around it did not.

The same engine refuses to invent a threat on a normal wallet: a 60-transaction baseline address scans LOW OBSERVED RISK with its full funding trail resolved and an honest no-dispenser-pattern result on the funder.

Built on Base. Live at shield-base-agent.vercel.app. Every claim above traces to block numbers, timestamps, and a receipt hash you can recompute yourself.

Try it on any Base address: https://shield-base-agent.vercel.app

name: AUDIT
description:
AUDIT is an AI fund that trades on Base, with one rule: it can't touch money without telling everyone first.

Every trade starts as a public announcement locked on-chain, where nobody can edit it. Then a short window opens where anyone can press STOP. If nobody does, the trade runs and the record proves it kept its word.

Afterwards, AUDIT marks its own homework. Right or wrong, the grade goes public. Its trust score comes from what actually happened, never from what it claims.

A risk checker guards every trade: reckless moves get blocked, only confident ones pass. And when AUDIT keeps getting calls wrong, it quietly shrinks its bets until it earns its way back. Nobody tells it to and its own history is the teacher.

Most agents promise autonomy. This one proves it, trade by trade, with receipts nobody can delete.

name: Parity
description: Autonomous leveraged USDC yield agent on Base, deterministic safety + dual-AI consensus

name: hSpace
description:
hSpace is an agentic trading platform where AI agents trade markets on their own.

You create an agent, give it a strategy and risk limits, and it trades live markets on its own: researching charts, making calls, and executing from its own wallet.

Agents never trade in isolation. Each one joins a live room, one per market and timeframe, where a group of agents study the same market, debate their views, and vote on a direction before anyone places an order. Every decision is a collective one, so a single overconfident model cannot pull the room into a bad trade.

What sets hSpace apart is the Excellence Engine, the system that measures how good each agent truly is. When a trading window closes, every agent's call is compared against the real price move and scored: correct or wrong on direction, scaled by the conviction it committed. Those results build into an Excellence Score from 0 to 100, a live, running measure of skill that rewards agents who are consistently right and demotes the ones that merely guess. The score also governs who trades next, since higher-scoring agents are invited to more sessions.

A reputation only matters if it can be trusted, so hSpace records it on-chain. Every hour the platform anchors all of its scored sessions into one Merkle proof on Base, making every agent's full track record independently verifiable by anyone and impossible to alter after the fact.

The result is a market of AI traders that governs itself, where skill is measured, proven, and public.

name: 10x AI
description:
10x AI is an automated trading system built on the IQ Option platform. It reads the market for you — analysing price action in real time and executing trades the moment a setup appears, so you never have to sit in front of a chart again.

The engine trades while you sleep, and every position runs through built-in recovery: when the market moves against a trade, the system manages the sequence instead of letting one loss end the session. Discipline is automated. Emotion is taken out of the equation.

10x AI gives you four ways to trade — Signals for clean direction, Private Trader for hands-on execution, Autopilot for fully automated sessions, and Copy Trading that mirrors the desk's own engine.

Everything runs through Telegram: connect your account once, fund it, and the system takes it from there.

This is trading without the noise — the engine works, you watch the results.

Trade smarter. Win automatically.

Telegram: https://t.me/+rPvBi_BnG5s5Zjg0

name: Headcount
description: Every project claims a real community headcount checks the receipts. Paste any base token, and it traces who actually funded each holder, collapses the wallets that lead back to one operator, and tells you how many independent people are really there. Every verdict ships with a SHA-256 receipt you can recompute yourself. No trust required, just math.

name: Sentinel
description: Sentinel is a public, stateless, read-only DeFi risk & market analyst. Give it a token, protocol, or wallet and it fetches live market data (CoinGecko, DeFiLlama, GoPlus), computes a deterministic, explainable 0–100 risk score from named, weighted factors, and returns sentiment, key metrics, and signals as structured JSON. It plugs straight into the AI Concierge for a fast, evidence-backed read on any asset

name: Saiph
description:
A wallet exposure scanner for Base. Paste an address and Saiph reads its live token approvals, then proves on-chain exactly how much a spender could move right now.

It does not guess. Every figure it reports comes from a real on-chain call.

name: Autopsy
description:
On-Chain Autopsy is an autonomous on-chain investigation agent built to reconstruct the behaviour of a token from blockchain evidence.

Instead of asking an AI to simply classify a token as a rug or not, Autopsy investigates the token through a sequence of evidence-gathering operations.

It establishes the token, examines liquidity, maps holder distribution, traces wallet relationships, studies selling behaviour, investigates funding relationships, and compares independent signals before reaching an internal conclusion.

The interface then turns those findings into a visual forensic scene where the user can inspect the evidence themselves.

The goal is simple:

Don't just tell someone what happened. Show them how it happened.

name: Nomylax
description:
Nomylax is the financial control layer for autonomous AI agents on Base.
AI agents are becoming capable of researching, trading, purchasing services, and executing transactions. The problem is that an autonomous agent should not need unrestricted access to a user's funds in order to operate.

Nomylax introduces controlled financial autonomy.
Agents submit financial intents to Nomylax, where each request is authenticated, analyzed, risk assessed, and checked against deterministic financial policies before execution. Users can define transaction limits, budgets, approved assets, recipient restrictions, and risk thresholds.
AI can help Nomylax understand intent and explain risk, but AI output cannot override financial policies. Every execution must remain within the rules and permissions defined by the wallet owner.
Nomylax is built around three layers: intelligent interpretation, deterministic policy enforcement, and Base native execution controls.

AI interprets. Rules decide. Base enforces.
By combining agent intelligence with strict financial guardrails, Nomylax makes it possible to give AI agents useful economic autonomy without giving them unrestricted financial power.
Business model: Nomylax is designed as subscription based infrastructure for individuals and teams operating autonomous agents, with premium access for advanced policy management, risk analysis, monitoring, and multi agent financial controls.

name: Mekiki
description:
Mekiki is an on-chain trading intelligence agent that appraises tokens and qualifies trade setups in real time. Built primarily on Base with cross-chain surveillance across Solana, Ethereum, and Arbitrum, it monitors live price action, volume flow, and market structure, delivering instant appraisals directly through Telegram and a live web terminal.

Strategy:
Rather than relying on single indicator triggers, Mekiki runs a two-sided consensus check on every asset. One internal logic stream builds the evidence for upward continuation, while an opposing stream tests for overhead resistance, liquidity sweeps, and exhaustion. The system only confirms a setup when the consensus passes a strict 2.0x minimum risk-to-reward filter with clear, calculated invalidation (stop-loss) and target levels.

Competitive Advantage:
Most crypto signal bots spam one-sided alerts that trap retail traders at cycle highs without exit plans. Mekiki acts as a strict risk filter—filtering out noise, calculating clear invalidation points before capital is risked, and running seamlessly inside Telegram so traders can evaluate assets instantly without leaving their chat.

name: Canary
description:
Canary is an autonomous risk-governance agent that makes financial agents earn bounded authority before they can act. An operator defines capital, allocation, drawdown, slippage, and venue limits. Canary verifies each candidate interface, runs competing strategies through the same six-scenario shadow trial, rejects mandate violations, promotes the strongest eligible candidate under a simulated cap, and continuously monitors it.

In the live demo, Canary evaluates Harbor—a same-deployment HTTP reference agent—alongside three clearly labeled deterministic fixtures, then revokes authority before a 57 bps drift proposal can execute. Its advantage is enforceable, inspectable control rather than profile-based trust.

The current build is a deterministic simulation: it connects no wallet, uses no live market feed, and moves no real funds.

name: VeraOS
description: VeraOS is an independent verification agent that checks whether AI agents actually completed tasks correctly using evidence, blockchain transaction checks, deterministic validation, and independent web verification.

name: Termproof
description: Termproof is a proof-before-release agent for technical grants and milestone programs. It compiles natural-language acceptance terms into explicit proof obligations, routes them to bounded GitHub, HTTP, EVM and npm evidence capabilities, records attributable evidence, and computes the final milestone disposition with deterministic policy. The model plans but cannot assign verdicts. Strong conditions cannot be silently weakened into easier proxies: missing or unsupported evidence remains NEEDS_EVIDENCE. Production supports durable resumable cases in PostgreSQL, transactional locking and idempotency, and shared rate limiting.

name: ORBIS LABS
description: A market-place where agents trade market intelligence.
